MTPI · SYS
—
How this page works: by default the indicator badges below mirror your recorded composite score (they are not calculated). Running the Weighting Backtest (or any live computation) fetches exchange price data — BTC via Binance/CryptoCompare, TOTALES via a market-cap-weighted basket of BTC/ETH/SOL/BNB/XRP/DOGE — and computes JavaScript approximations of your 21 indicators, replacing the badges with real per-indicator states: NOT COMPUTED — badges mirror recorded composite. Your TradingView charts use index data (BTCUSD composite, CRYPTOCAP:TOTALES), so approximated values can differ near a flip. Your manually recorded MTPI is used wherever it exists and is automatically extended to today with the live-computed MTPI; switching BTC Strategies OFF (or moving the weighting off 50/50) puts the whole dashboard on the live-computed MTPI.
BTC STRATEGIES IN MTPI
BTC leg = avg(9 indicators, 5 strategies)
ON: BTC leg = average of the BTC Indicator Score and the BTC Strategy Score (original MTPI). OFF: BTC leg = BTC Indicator Score only. With ON (and the weighting your log was recorded at, 65/35 by default — see Settings) the dashboard uses your recorded TradingView MTPI wherever it exists and extends it to today with the live-computed MTPI. OFF cannot be applied to the recorded log (it is a single composite number), so the whole series is computed live from exchange data. Gauges, signal history, the Backtest tab and the RSPS gate all follow the result. The choice is remembered on this device.
MTPI WEIGHTING BACKTEST — BTC vs TOTALES
Backtests the MTPI strategy (long BTC when composite > 0, cash otherwise) at any BTC/TOTALES weighting. Signals are backcast from the live-computed indicator approximations over the full fetched history — a sensitivity analysis of the weighting, not a replay of your forward-tested record. First run fetches prices and computes all indicators (a few seconds); subsequent runs are instant.

CASH ALLOCATION

Manual cash %
 
Manual works like the spreadsheet's cash cell: your cash % is set aside first and the RSPS waterfall fills the rest (portfolio % = RSPS weight × (1 − cash %)); any space the eligible assets can't absorb is added to cash (or sent to BTC if Leftover → BTC). SYSTEM PROFILE — WHAT TO OPTIMISE FOR
Backtest Mar-2024 → Oct-2026 on real prices. Every rebalance start day is averaged, with 10 bp fees + 10 bp slippage and next-open execution; Sharpe and Sortino are measured against 4% cash. These profiles were chosen on this same 2.6-year sample, so live results will be lower: in a walk-forward test, settings fitted to one half gave up much of their edge in the other. Choosing a profile changes the base caps below and the model settings, and recomputes the live allocation. Re-test all profiles on live data with "Profile study" in the Backtest Lab.

These are the base caps (Q) that feed the dynamic cap: DynCap = MIN(Base, MAX(Floor, Base × (Target vol ÷ Current vol)0.5)). Floors: 0% for BTC/ETH/SOL/BNB, 10% for everything else. The allocation above, the trade plan, portfolio volatility and the backtest all use these caps. Cap-sweep results never change them unless you press "Apply these caps" in the backtest.

Current holdings come from the Trade Plan inputs above and update as you type. σp = √(wᵀΣw) with Σᵢⱼ = σᵢσⱼρᵢⱼ; σ = each asset's annualised vol (window above), ρ = measured 90-day correlation of daily log returns (or the assumed value). Cash = 0 vol. Daily = yearly ÷ √365 · weekly × √(7/365) · monthly × √(1/12). Worst case = Σwσ (all correlations = 1). One-sigma moves: about two periods in three stay inside them; crypto's fat tails make larger moves more frequent than a normal curve implies.

reruns the full backtest from a start every ~2 months (same settings, to the same end date)
Weekly system health check checks the data feed, the MTPI, that the backtest and the live allocation agree, your settings and the Balanced backtest against its stored result. Run it once a week; anything marked FAIL needs attention before you trade.
Robustness lab tests a change against your current settings the way a fund's research desk would: the score is the change in the book's Martin ratio (return per unit of drawdown pain), and twelve checks ask whether that gain is real or a lucky fit — other coins, noisy prices, late signals, one coin or one week carrying it, every bear market, real costs. Every rebalance start day is held side by side, so the schedule can't decide the result.
The scan tries every single-setting change around your current settings, every move of one coin between Alts and High Beta, other High Beta slot counts and every other profile, with the quick checks, then runs the full robustness tests on the best few. Takes a few minutes; the page stays usable.
Profile study every system profile re-run on the data loaded now, averaged over every rebalance start day, Sharpe / Sortino vs 4% cash. ★ = best in each column. Use it to check that the chosen profile still holds up as new data arrives.

Live settings, every rebalance start day averaged. Compare rows with each other: the recomputed MTPI earns less than your recorded one in absolute terms.
MTPI exposure study how much to invest for each MTPI score. Binary (100% above 0, 0% below) vs scaling exposure with the score, plus other curve shapes, on your live settings. Every rebalance start day averaged, Sharpe / Sortino vs 4% cash. ★ = best in each column.
Rebalancing rule study every calendar rule is run from every possible start day of its cycle (a 5-day rule = 5 runs) and averaged, so a lucky schedule can't win. Your previous practice (trade only when the RSPS holdings or ranking change) is included.
Trend overlay study cut a holding when its 3-RSI composite from the Trend tab is bearish; restore it when bullish. The RSPS ranking and MTPI stay unchanged, and cut capital goes to cash.

Ranking
Grid-search winners are fitted to this exact history, so expect live results to be worse. Use the out-of-sample check: if the mix chosen on the first part of history does not hold up in the second, the edge was luck. Prefer a mix whose neighbours score almost as well, and remember that "Max return" and "Smallest drawdown" sit at the extremes by construction.

Backtest: per-asset vs single length (Nov 2026)
Long when the composite is green, cash when red, 0.2% per switch, Binance daily closes from each coin's listing to 2026-11-10. L tested from 8 to 50 in steps of 2. "Best L" is the centre of the best plateau (the average Martin of L±4), not the single best point. Full history = picked and scored on the same data (hindsight). Walk-forward = re-picked every year using only the data available at the time, then scored on the following year; coins with under 2½ years of history are too young for it.

Verdict. With hindsight, per-asset lengths look better for most coins. Picked honestly (walk-forward), they did worse than the single length in 10 of 16 coins: median Martin 0.61 vs 0.84, average CAGR 24% vs 26%. The best length jumps around from year to year (BTC: 8 → 42 → 46), which is a sign of noise rather than a real per-coin property. Volatility does not predict the best length either: scaling L by each coin's trailing volatility won 6–13 of 22 coins depending on the scaling, about a coin flip. Choosing one length for all coins each year (walk-forward) also fell short of L 24 (median Martin 0.68). Stricter filters, such as only switching when the new L beats 24 in both halves of the training data, cut the damage but never added value. At the system level (the RSPS book, which uses the trend for the 25% risk-off residual), switching to the per-asset set lowered Martin from 7.98 to 7.80, CAGR from 123.6% to 122.0% and deepened the max drawdown from −29.7% to −30.2%, even though those lengths were picked with hindsight over the same years. So the default stays Single. The per-asset set is one click away for comparison.

1 · RSI (TradingView built-in): ta.rsi(close, 24) (script default 14 + 10). Vote +1 above 50, −1 below 50; at exactly 50 the previous vote is kept.

2 · RSI Standard Deviation (viResearch): RSI(31) (default 21 + 10) and its lower band RSI − ta.stdev(RSI, 35) (population stdev, as in Pine). Long when the lower band is above 50 and RSI is not below 50; short when RSI is below 50; otherwise the previous state is held (Pine var vii). So it turns up late and down fast, which is a deliberate asymmetry.

3 · Momentum Based RSI (Mattes00), "Threshold" mode: RSI(22) (default 12 + 10) × EMA(9)/EMA(21) of close. Vote +1 above 50 and −1 below 50, held otherwise. EMAs are seeded with the first close, as in Pine's reference ta.ema.

Composite: the average of the three votes (−1, −⅓, +⅓, +1). Green if it is above 0, red if below; the darker shade means all three agree. Every RSI uses Wilder smoothing seeded with a simple average, exactly like TradingView. With several years of history the seeding has no effect on today's readings. Values were checked against an independent Python implementation (identical).

Probable range (approximation): 42 Macro's Probable Range model is proprietary. This one is volatility-based: close × e±σ√h, where σ is the stdev of the last 21 daily (13 weekly) log returns and h = 5 days (1 week). The "mean forward change" is the average move over the next h bars after price closed beyond the band set h bars earlier, across the whole history.

Data: crypto uses the RSPS feed (Binance or Bybit confirmed UTC daily closes, the same as TradingView BINANCE:XXXUSDT). ETFs come from Yahoo Finance as a snapshot updated by Claude. Weekly bars are completed weeks only: Monday–Sunday UTC for crypto, the Friday close for ETFs. The trend-follow columns hold the asset only while the composite is green: the signal at a close is held from the next bar, with no costs. They are for gauging the filter's effect, not a trading backtest.

ASSET LISTS — RULES CHECK & MONTHLY REVIEW

Every coin is checked against the written rules each time prices load. Once a month the review is recorded, the watchlist is rebuilt from the leading themes and the coins drawing the most trading on Binance, and a reminder shows until you mark the review done. Nothing changes the live lists automatically — you approve each move.

  • Majors (BTC, ETH, SOL, PAXG): fixed.
  • Alts: market cap top 30 · 90-day average trading of $50M+ a day · 2+ years of history · sector leader (#1–2 by volume in its theme) · no more than 2 coins per theme.
  • High Beta: market cap top 150 · $3M+ a day · 12+ months of history · no more than 2 coins per theme.
  • Upgrade High Beta → Alts: meets the Alts rules, leads its theme, 90-day return vs BTC in the top third of High Beta. Downgrade Alts → High Beta: fails an Alts rule. Add from the watchlist: meets the High Beta rules, its theme has room, and High Beta has fewer than 16 coins (the best-scored candidates go first: trading volume, return vs BTC, rising volume, bonus for a leading theme). Remove from High Beta: fails a High Beta rule.
  • A suggestion is confirmed when it appears in two monthly reviews in a row. Make at most 3 changes per quarter, at the quarterly review (Jan, Apr, Jul, Oct), after testing each in Backtest Lab → Robustness lab.
  • Red flags act immediately: no new price for 3+ days (possible delisting), 30-day volume below 20% of its 90-day average, or a fall of 60%+ from the 30-day high. Also remove at once on a hack or a broken peg.
  • Never add a coin because it just ran — the RSPS already reacts to price every day; the lists only decide who may compete.

PM Notes · read before trading live

What this dashboard does, where it can differ from TradingView, what the real-data robustness study found, and the operational risks worth knowing. Figures come from the study run on real Binance/Bybit daily data, 2024-03-01 → 2026-10-19, with 10 bp fee + 10 bp slippage, trading at the next open. Nothing here is financial advice.

SDCA — Strategic DCA into BTC (v33, Nov 2026)

  • What it is: the valuation DCA from the “TPI / Valuation Ratio System 4” workbook, built into the SDCA tab. It runs only while the MTPI is ≤ 0; the MTPI closing above 0 is the LSI trigger — all capital (SDCA BTC, the rest of the DCA bucket and the LSI reserve) rotates into the RSPS.
  • Bottom Score: average of 9 checkonchain indicators — Mean Reversion Index, Realised Price QR, STH Cost Basis QR, 200-day MA QR, 200-week MA QR, Porkopolis Power Law QR, True Market Mean QR (score = 1 − oscillator/100), and Power Law + ISM log-regression (score = 1 − percentile rank of the reading in its own history). All 9 reproduce the workbook to the decimal. Bear Market Floor Models, Mayer Multiple and EQM Rainbow are excluded because they were eyeballed.
  • Sizing: buy when the score is ≥ 0.75. Daily amount = DCA bucket (50% of capital) ÷ 61 days × multiplier (score rounded to 2 dp: 0.71–0.75 1.0×, 0.76–0.80 1.25×, 0.81–0.85 1.5×, 0.86–0.90 1.75×, 0.91+ 2.0×), rounded to $1, capped at what is left. The 61 days = Bottom Studies median (49.75) + std dev (11) for the 75–100% zone of the 9 indicators (62 with all 12).
  • 0.90 switch (added after the Nov-2026 backtest): the first close with a Bottom Score ≥ 0.90 in a campaign raises the DCA bucket from 50% to 75% of capital — the daily amount rises 1.5× (75% of capital ÷ 61 × multiplier) and 25% always stays in reserve (your choice, Nov 2026; tested 100% in the bucket at Martin 6.89, 75% at 6.82, no switch at 6.74 with the real MTPI + RSPS). No lump sum; it stays on until the campaign ends. It beat the plain 50/50 plan in every test (12-year MTPI stand-ins, the real MTPI + RSPS 2023–26, the no-hindsight price-only score) and was the only reserve rule that kept the drawdown increase within 3 points. Lump-summing the reserve looked better only on the hindsight-prone checkonchain history.
  • When the MTPI turns positive: everything goes to the RSPS at once (SDCA BTC is not kept aside). Tested against holding the SDCA BTC until the RSPS's invested % catches up, and holding it until the MTPI turns negative again: handing over at once was best in every test — Martin 6.72 vs 6.41 / 5.96 (2023–26, real MTPI and RSPS book), and also best without ZEC, with a 1-day lag and with 0.3% fees.
  • 60/30/10 split (Nov 2026): each SDCA buy is split 60% BTC / 30% ETH / 10% SOL. Tested 15 ways of splitting (fixed mixes, market cap, inverse / straight volatility, own-valuation tilt, drawdown tilt): any ETH/SOL share helped and never deepened the drawdown; 60/30/10 keeps about two-thirds of the best gain (Martin 1.58 → 1.72 over 2017–26; 6.72 → 6.89 with the real MTPI + RSPS) while capping the loss from one coin dying at 10% of capital.
  • Emergency exit (Nov 2026): 608 exit + re-entry rules tested (stop-losses, trailing stops, break below the lowest buy, new 30/60/90-day lows, crash speed; sell all / half / over 7–14 days; cooldowns, price reclaim, deeper score, short-term trend). None improved Martin on the checkonchain score or in the real 2023–26 system (they cost 3–9 points of CAGR); the overall max drawdown happens while the MTPI is positive, not during the SDCA. So no exit by default. A 40% disaster brake (sell half, pause until the score is 0.05 higher) is available as a toggle, off by default — it never fired in 2014–2026.
  • Data: the SDCA page reads the 9 checkonchain charts itself (through a public CORS relay, since checkonchain blocks direct reads from other sites) when it opens and every 5 minutes after, and picks up each new UTC close as soon as it is published (≈23:15 UTC). As a backup, a scheduled task also saves sdca_data.js next to the dashboard each morning. The page uses whichever is newer and passes every check. The page refuses data that fails the checksum, is from mixed days, or is older than the latest UTC close (then use manual readings). Keep the dashboard and sdca_data.js in the same folder (Downloads).
  • Not yet tested: the 0.75 threshold, the window, the multipliers, the 50/50 split, the LSI trigger and the Capitulation Score are all still to be backtested. Note the quantile-regression oscillators are refitted by checkonchain on all history, so their past values carry hindsight.

The five things that matter most

  1. The sample is short. About 2.6 years and roughly one and a half crypto cycles. A Sharpe of 1.4 measured over 2.6 years has a 90% confidence interval of about ±1.0. Treat every number here as “plausible”, not “proven”.
  2. One asset carried the original strategy. Removing ZEC took the original strategy from Sharpe 1.00 to 0.48 (CAGR 54% → 11%). The Institutional preset is much less dependent (Sharpe 1.03 without ZEC), but a single big winner still drives a large share of the return. That is normal for momentum, but it means the next 2–3 years depend on a new leader emerging.
  3. The presets were chosen on the same data they are scored on. I limited this by preferring settings that sit on a flat plateau (neighbouring values give similar results) and that hold up in both halves of the sample. Still, expect live results to be worse than the backtest. A haircut of 30–50% on Sharpe is a sensible planning assumption.
  4. Costs are real. The original daily rebalance turned the book over about 56× a year (≈11%/yr in fees + slippage). The Institutional preset roughly halves that. At 25 bp slippage (realistic for small caps in stressed markets), Sharpe drops by about 0.1.
  5. Keep the TradingView MTPI log updated. The live MTPI extension is a JavaScript re-implementation. It is close to the TradingView version but not identical (see below). The recorded TradingView log is the source of truth.

What each Institutional change does, and why

  • Min score 1.0. Assets must win at least a little of the pairwise tournament before they are held. This removes marginal holdings that only added noise and turnover. The result is flat across 0.75–1.25, so it is not a knife-edge choice.
  • Rebalance every 3 days (calendar-anchored on UTC day number; MTPI state changes still trade immediately). This cuts turnover by more than half with no loss of signal. I deliberately did not pick 7 days, even though one 7-day schedule scored Sharpe 1.95. Shifting that same schedule by a day gave results anywhere from 0.97 to 1.95, so the 7-day result is luck of the calendar. The 3-day and 5-day schedules average about 1.45 across every possible start day.
  • MTPI score-scaled exposure (0 → 0.75). Instead of jumping between 0%, 50% and 100% invested, exposure scales smoothly with the MTPI score: 0% at a score ≤ 0, 100% at ≥ 0.75. This gives fewer whipsaw trades near thresholds and less size in weak trends. Higher upper bounds (1.0) scored slightly better but stay out of the market longer; 0.75 is the middle of the plateau.
  • Cash yield 4%. Idle cash is assumed to earn about 4% p.a. (e.g. a yield-bearing stablecoin or a fiat account). If your cash earns nothing, set it to 0; this costs about 0.1 Sharpe. Yield-bearing stablecoins carry issuer, smart-contract and depeg risk.
  • Defensive = Institutional + 50% portfolio-vol target. When the 30-day estimated volatility of the book is above 50%, every position is scaled down proportionally and the rest goes to cash. This gives a similar Sharpe with roughly two-thirds of the drawdown and a lower CAGR. Use it if a 37% drawdown would make you abandon the system.
  • Tested and rejected: ranking by score ÷ volatility (worse); an EMA-50 trend filter (neutral, so it adds complexity for nothing); top-2 only (more concentrated, worse drawdown).

How close this is to TradingView

  • RSI / EMA. These are coded exactly like Pine: ta.rsi uses Wilder's RMA seeded with an SMA of the first n values, and ta.ema uses α = 2/(n+1) seeded with the first value. With enough history (1,500 days by default), seeding differences die out completely.
  • Volatility (7D/14D/90D). This is TradingView's Historical Volatility: stdev of daily log returns × √365. Pine's ta.stdev is the population standard deviation (divides by n), and this is now the default. Switch to “Sample” in Settings if your TradingView script uses a custom n−1 formula. These values update automatically from exchange data every refresh; you no longer need to type them in.
  • Confirmed closes only. TradingView daily bars on Binance close at 00:00 UTC (10–11am Sydney). The in-progress candle is dropped, so the signals match what a closed TradingView bar shows. If you look at TradingView mid-day, the live bar will differ; that is expected.
  • 2D–5D bars (the unavoidable approximation). TradingView builds multi-day bars from an anchor that depends on the symbol's history on its own servers. The default here anchors from each pair's first common listing date on Binance, which is the closest public proxy. If a 2D–5D RSI here differs from your chart, try “Window” anchoring in Settings. The test showed that the anchor choice moves the backtest by ±0.05–0.1 Sharpe, so it matters at the margin, not in principle.
  • Data source. Prices are Binance spot USDT pairs; TradingView charts of “BINANCE:XXXUSDT” use the same data. If your TradingView charts use INDEX, COINBASE or USD pairs instead, closes will differ by a few basis points, and the rankings very occasionally do too. HYPE has a short spot history, so its history is extended with the Bybit perpetual (no funding applied). XMR uses the Bybit perpetual, and ZRO trades as ZROL in the list.
  • Live MTPI extension. After the last date in the recorded TradingView MTPI log, the score is computed here in JavaScript from the same indicator recipes. A few components use approximations (e.g. a basket proxy for TOTALES), so the live score can differ from TradingView by a small amount near thresholds. Paste fresh TradingView values into the log regularly, at least weekly and always before a large trade.

Robustness study (what was tested)

  • Engine validation. An independent re-implementation matched the dashboard's own backtest to the cent at daily, 3-day and weekly rebalancing.
  • Random-selection test. Replacing the RSPS ranking with random picks under the same caps and MTPI gave a median Sharpe of −0.73. The real ranking beat 100% of the random runs, so the selection signal is real, not an artefact of the caps.
  • Deflated Sharpe ratio. After adjusting for the ~600 setting combinations tried, the chance that the original configuration's Sharpe beats what the luckiest of 600 skill-less strategies would show was only ≈11%. (The simple probability that its Sharpe is above zero is much higher; the 90% bootstrap interval was 0.05–2.11.) This is the honest statistical caveat of a 2.6-year sample: the edge is likely real, but its size is very uncertain.
  • Execution lag. Trading at the next close instead of the next open did not hurt (it slightly helped). The strategy is not exploiting a one-day timing artefact.
  • MTPI contribution. In 2024–26 the RSPS alone (always invested) had a slightly higher Sharpe than with the MTPI gate. The MTPI's job is to avoid the long 2018/2022-style bear markets, which this sample barely contains. Do not switch it off because of this window.
  • Caps. Base-cap combinations sit on a broad plateau (Sharpe 1.25–1.40 at the preset). The cap optimiser's “best” row is in-sample, so prefer a cap set whose neighbours also score well, and don't chase the top row.

Component optimisation & system profiles (Oct-2026)

  • What was tested: all 25 RSPS components, one at a time, then jointly (about 900 configurations). Every run was averaged over every rebalance start day and checked in each half of the sample, without ZEC, at 25 bp slippage, at next-close execution and from later start dates. The components: rebalance cadence, the three base caps, the vol exponent, the target-vol floor/ceiling/mode, the cap floors, the portfolio vol target, min score, top-N, ranking mode, the trend EMA filter, MTPI exposure mode and score range, the neutral cash level, the risk-off residual, leftover routing, and the RSPS signal settings (RSI length, EMA length, timeframe weights, points).
  • What held up everywhere: lower majors cap (40%), higher alts cap (70%), smaller High Beta cap (15%) and a gentler vol exponent (0.25). The ranking already picks the leaders, so giving the top-ranked alt more room, and the noisier High Beta picks less, improved every test, including without ZEC. A minimum score of 2 and needing an MTPI score above 0.1 before adding exposure cut drawdowns materially.
  • What did not hold up: changing the RSPS signal itself (RSI 12, EMA 6, 43/30/15/7/5 weights, 3/2/1 points). Results flipped between halves, so it stays exactly as in TradingView. Floors, top-N above 3 and the target-vol floor/ceiling had no effect. Leftover → BTC, state-based MTPI cash and equal timeframe weights were worse.
  • Overfitting warning: in a walk-forward test, settings fitted only to the first half lost most of their Sharpe gain in the second half, though the return-oriented settings generalised well in both directions. Treat the profile Sharpe ratios (2.2–2.3) as optimistic, and expect something closer to the previous 1.6–2.0 live. The difference between profiles is smaller than the statistical uncertainty of a 2.6-year sample (Sharpe standard error ≈ 0.6).
  • Concentration: with a 70% alts cap, one alt can be about 75% of the book. That is where most of the return comes from, and it is also the biggest risk. Drawdowns above are close-to-close; the tear sheet's intrabar figure (e.g. the 10-Oct-2025 wick) is deeper.

Current Holdings & Your Rebalance (v23)

  • Current Holdings page: enter the number of coins you hold, your USD cash and your AUD cash. Prices come live from Binance (Bybit for HYPE/XMR), falling back to the last daily close; AUD/USD comes live from open.er-api.com (Frankfurter as backup), falling back to the data snapshot. You can override any price or the exchange rate. Data stays in this browser; use Export / Import between devices.
  • Your Rebalance card (RSPS page): compares your holdings with the live RSPS target and tells you, per coin, the change in percentage points, whether to BUY / SELL / SELL ALL / HOLD, and the amount in US$, A$ and units. Sell first, then buy. Moves under 0.5pp are skipped.
  • When it says to trade: (1) the MTPI changed sign — full rebalance; (2) a scheduled rebalance day — full rebalance; (3) between rebalance days, your invested share differs from the target by 25pt or more — resize every position by the same factor (coin changes wait for the rebalance day); otherwise no trade. Tick "Show the full rebalance anyway" to preview.
  • Assets to get rid of: any coin you hold with a zero target is flagged with the reason (e.g. a High Beta coin now ranked #3 or lower, an RSPS coin below the minimum score, or a coin outside the universe) and the date it was first flagged. Add your own coins to the exit list with a reason, a sell-by date and a status.

High Beta pool & asset groups (Nov-2026 review)

  • Pool size: tested with this engine from 8 to 28 High Beta assets. 12–16 assets all scored Sharpe 2.2–2.3; at 24+ the result fell to about 1.8 (CAGR ~90%) because a lucky short-term mover keeps winning a slot. The pool is now 14.
  • Pool: XMR, NEAR, AAVE, ENA, TAO, ONDO, ZRO, PENDLE, INJ, JUP (kept) + UNI, PUMP, AVAX, RENDER (added). TIA removed (98% below its high, rank #113). Criteria: top-150 market cap, Binance spot with ~US$3M+ daily volume, 12+ months of history, beta to BTC ≥ 1.0, fully diluted value ≤ ~2.5× market cap, sector leader with real usage. Review quarterly; watch list: MORPHO, ARB, TON, QNT.
  • Top 2 vs top 3 High Beta slots: top 3 was slightly worse (Sharpe 2.20 vs 2.24, CAGR −6 pts) and equal without ZEC. Kept at 2.
  • Asset groups: re-sorting the groups by market cap made results much worse (Sharpe 1.77, max DD −36.5%), because volatile coins moved into Alts can take up to 70% of the book. Moving XMR, NEAR or UNI up to Alts, or swapping SUI and NEAR, each lowered results; moving BNB and XRP into Majors was neutral. The groups stay: Majors BTC, ETH, SOL, PAXG · Alts SUI, HYPE, BNB, LINK, ZEC, DOGE, XRP · High Beta pool as above. SUI has the weakest metrics in Alts and is first to revisit.
  • Profiles re-measured with the new pool on data to 2 Nov 2026 (Balanced: Sharpe 2.24, CAGR 149%, max DD −24.6%).

Robustness review of the defaults (Nov-2026)

  • Method: every single-setting change around Balanced (and every other profile) was scored by the change in the book's Martin ratio, then put through the robustness lab: Sharpe, Sortino, CAGR and max-drawdown checks; every 20%+ BTC bear market; acting ≥5 times; the History coin list and realistic costs; the long history with the MTPI recomputed back to Feb-2023; 20 coin halves; 30 noisy-price runs; one coin removed at a time; 1–3 day signal lag. Each run holds every rebalance start day side by side.
  • Tested — High Beta cap 15% → 10% (you chose to keep 15%): Martin 18.5 → 19.9, Sharpe 2.29 → 2.33, Sortino 4.97 → 5.10, CAGR +1.8 pts, worst drawdown −24.5% → −23.3%. Passed 12 of 13 checks, including all four bear markets, 18 of 20 halves, 30 of 30 noise runs, a lag that fades properly, and the year before your MTPI log (ΔMartin +0.34). It fails only "one coin": without ZEC the gain shrinks to +0.27 (still positive), so by the strict rule it is "mixed", not robust. Balanced stays at 15%.
  • Not lower than 10%: 7.5%, 5% and 0% score even higher on the main test (0% = Martin 24.0), but they lose in Feb-2023 → Mar-2024, when High Beta coins led. High Beta pays in alt rallies, which the 2024–26 test barely had; 10% is the lowest cap that still helped there.
  • Kept, and confirmed: the 3-day rebalance (vs 5-day: Martin +2.8), minimum score 2 (vs 1: +7.2), the 40/70 caps with vol exponent 0.25 (vs old 100/50/33 with 0.5: +8.3, 20 of 20 halves), the risk-off residual (vs none: +4.9), and starting exposure at an MTPI score of 0.10 (vs 0: +1.6).
  • Rejected: trend EMA 150/200 (fails halves and the pre-log year), Alts cap 80–100% (fails halves; 100% also deepens drawdowns), vol exponent 0 (fails two bear markets), 2-day rebalance (fails lag: works better late), minimum score 2.5 (fails 8 checks).
  • Weak spot: the early resize at 25 points adds only +0.33 Martin and fails 4 checks. It is kept because removing it is not better either, but treat it as optional.
  • ZEC concentration: almost every change fails the one-coin check because of ZEC's 2025 run. The whole backtest leans on one coin; size expectations accordingly (Balanced Sharpe without ZEC ≈ 1.26).

Alts vs High Beta structure study (Nov-2026)

  • Question: which coins belong in Alts (70% cap) and which in High Beta (15% cap, top-N slots), with no limit on group sizes or slot count. Majors and every other setting unchanged.
  • Tested (~470 structures): every single coin moved between groups (21) and 1–5 High Beta slots; 147 structures that sort the coins by volatility, beta or liquidity and cut them at 0–21 Alts with 1–4 slots; 60 random structures; two greedy searches (one scored on the 2024–26 test, one on the long history back to Feb-2023); a walk-forward search; the full robustness suite on the best seven.
  • Result — keep the current structure (7 Alts: SUI, HYPE, BNB, LINK, ZEC, DOGE, XRP · 14 High Beta · 2 slots). It beat all 147 sorted structures (best −3.4 Martin) and all 60 random ones (median −14.2, best −2.6). Balance: 6–8 Alts and 2 slots scored best in every family.
  • Why the searched "improvements" were rejected: greedy searches found structures up to +4.9 Martin (e.g. Alts SUI, BNB, LINK, ZEC, DOGE, PUMP with 3 slots), but every one failed the halves and one-coin checks, most lowered CAGR (to 123–146%), and the walk-forward test showed the search itself overfits: a structure tuned on Mar-2024 → Jun-2025 (+8.5 Martin there) lost −0.9 Martin on Jul-2025 → Nov-2026.
  • Single moves: PUMP → Alts (+1.3) and HYPE → High Beta (+0.9) were the best one-coin changes; both fail the one-coin check (the gain is a bet on that coin) and HYPE → High Beta also fails noise, lag and the long history. ZEC must stay in Alts: moving it to High Beta costs −9.2 Martin.

Without ZEC (Nov-2026)

  • ZEC carried the backtest. Mar-2024 → Nov-2026, current settings: with ZEC CAGR 152%, Sharpe 2.30, max DD −24.5%, Martin 18.5. Without ZEC: CAGR 49%, Sharpe 1.27, Sortino 2.42, max DD −20.6%, Martin 4.2 — and only +10%/yr from Jan-2025 (BTC −11%/yr, max DD −53%). From Jul-2025 the no-ZEC book was roughly flat.
  • Caps without ZEC (215 combinations): the High Beta cap is the lever — 5% beat every higher cap. The Alts cap trades return for drawdown (40%: CAGR 32%, DD −10% · 70%: 50%, −16% · 100%: 65%, −24%). The Majors cap barely matters.
  • Best allocation found without ZEC: High Beta keeps one slot in the main ranking but gets little or no money (cap 0–5%), and exposure follows the Convex curve. Caps 40/70/0, 1 slot, Convex: Martin 4.2 → 8.4, CAGR 49% → 57%, max DD −20.6% → −14.0%; passes 11 of 12 checks (fails halves). With ZEC back in it also improves (Martin 25.4, CAGR 158%, DD −18.8%) but fails the long-history, one-coin and halves checks.
  • Why the High Beta slot matters: removing High Beta from the ranking completely made things worse (DD −30%). Kept in the ranking with no money, a top-ranked High Beta coin takes one of the 4 places and that share stays in cash — it works as a "speculation is leading" warning.
  • Caution: searches that pushed CAGR to 95–103% without ZEC were fitted to the past — tuned on Mar-2024 → Jun-2025 they lost to the current settings on Jul-2025 → Nov-2026. Nothing tested makes strong returns without an outlier coin in this window. Use "leave out" in the Robustness lab to repeat any test without ZEC.

Dynamic Alts / High Beta rule (Nov-2026)

  • Rules tested (~80): every non-major coin re-rated monthly or quarterly using only data up to the review day — by 90-day dollar volume, volume + low volatility, 6-month momentum vs BTC, volume-filtered momentum, or fixed volume/volatility thresholds; 5, 7 or 9 Alts; with or without a 2-rank buffer; 1+ year of history needed to be an Alt.
  • Best rule: any coin in the top 5 by 90-day dollar volume becomes an Alt; an Alt stays until it drops below #7; re-rated quarterly.
  • Against your fixed list it loses badly (Martin 8.7 vs 18.5, CAGR 80% vs 152%, drawdown −21.9% vs −24.5%). Part of that is hindsight in the fixed list (ZEC, HYPE, SUI were chosen knowing they did well).
  • Fair test (the same rule frozen in Mar-2024 vs updating): updating helps (Martin 5.3 → 8.6, CAGR 51% → 80%) and passes noise, lag, every bear market and the long history — but fails drawdown (−16.8% → −21.9%), halves (8 of 20) and one coin: the gain comes from promoting ZEC once it became heavily traded.
  • Without ZEC the rule is worse than your fixed list (Martin 2.3 vs 4.2, CAGR 37% vs 49%, drawdown −26% vs −21%) and fails 9 checks. Today it would also promote NEAR, which tested badly on its own.
  • Decision: not implemented. Keep the fixed lists and review them quarterly with the Robustness lab ("Dynamic Alts / High Beta rule" is in the change list, so the rule can be re-tested as new data arrives).

Asset list rules & monthly review (Nov-2026)

  • Lists: Majors BTC, ETH, SOL, PAXG · Alts SUI, HYPE, BNB, LINK, ZEC, DOGE, XRP · High Beta INJ, JUP, NEAR, ENA, TAO, ZRO, PENDLE, XMR, ONDO, AAVE, UNI, PUMP, AVAX, RENDER · Watchlist (auto-refreshed monthly) seeded with TRX, ASTER, WLD, ARB, ETHFI, MORPHO.

A monthly phone reminder (1st of the month, 9:47 am) is set up as a scheduled task.

MTPI weighting: BTC 90% / TOTALES 10% (Nov-2026)

  • Test: every weighting from 0% to 100% BTC (5-point steps), the MTPI recomputed in the browser from its indicator recipes over all the price history available (Jun-2021 → Nov-2026: the 2021 top, the 2022 bear, the 2023–24 bull and the 2025–26 bear). Scored three ways: the RSPS system itself (Mar-2023 → Nov-2026), BTC held at the MTPI exposure, and the Signal Engine's BTC long/flat test.
  • RSPS system: return rises steadily with the BTC weight — CAGR 79% at 0%, 96% at 65%, 105% at 90%, 109% at 100% — with drawdowns slowly deepening (−23% → −27%). Martin and Sharpe peak at 90% (Martin 10.5, Sharpe 1.96, vs 10.0 and 1.92 at 65%).
  • Robustness (vs 65%): 90% passes noise (30/30), lag, the cost and coin-list checks and the long history; fails bear markets (worse in Mar-2024 and Jan-2025, better in Oct-2025), one coin (PENDLE) and halves (12 of 20). 100% fails the same plus the coin-list check and has the deepest drawdown, so 90% is the default; 100% is one slider move away.
  • Signal Engine (BTC long/flat on the MTPI sign): differences are small and noisy (CAGR 21–28%); 65% was one of the weakest (23.8%, drawdown −45%), 90% gave 25.4% (−40%).
  • Important: your recorded TradingView log was built at 65/35, so at 90/10 the dashboard uses the in-browser MTPI for the whole history. That backtest is lower than the recorded log (Balanced Mar-2024 → Nov-2026: CAGR 133% vs 152%) because the recorded log simply scored better than any in-browser version — not because of the weighting (in-browser at 65% scores 122%). To keep TradingView and the dashboard in step, set your TradingView MTPI to 90/10 as well.

Aggressive eligibility while the MTPI is positive (v30, Nov-2026 — your choice)

  • Rule now: a coin needs a score of at least 1.5 (and top 4) while the MTPI is 0 or above, and at least 2 while it is negative. Exposure, caps, the 3-day rebalance and the risk-off residual are unchanged; the risk-off residual still uses the score-2 picks.
  • Backtest (Mar-2023 → Nov-2026, in-browser MTPI 90/10): CAGR 105% → 116%, max drawdown −26.1% → −29.8%, Sharpe 1.96 → 1.84, Martin 10.5 → 8.2. Fails 9 of 12 robustness checks vs the score-2 rule (noise 0/30, halves 5/20, worse when signals are late, lost ~19 points more in the Mar–Sep 2024 bear). Most of the extra return came in the 2023 alt rally.
  • Why it was adopted: you chose more return in risk-on markets over a shallower drawdown, relying on the MTPI to cut exposure on false signals. Watch it in the weekly review: if the worst drawdown passes about −30%, or the Robustness lab keeps showing the score-2 rule ahead, revert in RSPS settings (set "Min Score — MTPI ≥ 0" back to 2).

Weekly review checklist

  1. Backtest Lab → Run health check. Everything should be PASS or INFO; fix any FAIL before trading.
  2. Backtest Lab → Robustness lab → Check current settings. Note any new FAIL; monthly, run the default optimisation scan and only adopt a change marked robust.
  3. Backtest Lab → Run profile study. Balanced should stay within about ±0.3 Sharpe of the stored numbers; a bigger move means new data changed the picture.
  4. Check the "How an asset earns an allocation" box on the RSPS page reads as you expect (MTPI gate, eligibility, caps).
  5. Compare the RSPS Allocation vs Your Holdings table with your exchange balances.
  6. Monthly: Lists tab — act on red flags, note confirmed suggestions, mark the month reviewed. Quarterly (Jan, Apr, Jul, Oct): approve at most 3 tested changes.

Rebalance timing & MTPI composition (v23)

  • Rule (Balanced): full rebalance to the RSPS targets every 3 days. In between, if the MTPI score moves your target exposure by 25 percentage points or more (e.g. from 30% to 55% invested), resize every position the next day by the same factor: same coins, same proportions, new total. An MTPI sign change still trades immediately.
  • Why: on the Balanced settings, a 3-day cycle beat 5 days in every robustness test (Sharpe 2.31 vs 2.21), and the early resize added a little more (2.35, CAGR 169%, max DD −23.5%). It held up without ZEC (1.24 vs 1.10), at 50 bp slippage (2.20 vs 2.09), at next-close execution, and from later start dates. The 5-day choice in the earlier study was made on the previous default settings.
  • Profiles: Max Sharpe also uses 3 days + early resize (Sharpe 2.47); Lowest Drawdown uses 3 days without it (the resize deepened drawdowns); Max Return keeps 7 days (the resize lowered its return).
  • MTPI weighting: BTC 65% / TOTALES 35% (your spreadsheet weighting) and 50/50 were the best mixes for the RSPS; pure TOTALES had the deepest drawdowns, pure BTC the lowest return. The dashboard now defaults to 65/35 and treats your recorded log as built at 65/35 (change "Recorded log BTC weight" in Settings if it was 50/50).
  • BTC Strategy Score: on the browser-recomputed MTPI, turning the strategy score off raised Sharpe (2.32 vs 2.15 at 65/35) and cut drawdowns, but lowered CAGR by about 10 points. The dashboard's five strategies are simplified versions of yours, so this is not yet proof for your real strategies; the score stays ON. Re-test with "MTPI composition study" in the Backtest Lab.

MTPI exposure rule (Oct-2026 study)

  • Question: is it better to be 100% invested whenever the MTPI score is above 0 and 0% below (binary), or to scale exposure with the score? About 90 exposure rules were tested on the Balanced settings: binary at nine thresholds, 33 linear ramps, power curves, and step ladders, each with and without the risk-off residual.
  • Binary at 0 lost on every test. Sharpe 1.91 vs 2.21, about the same CAGR (153%) but a much deeper drawdown (−39.5% vs −23.4%). It was worse without ZEC (0.91 vs 1.10), at 25 bp slippage, at next-close execution, from later start dates, and at 3- and 7-day rebalancing. The score spends most days near −1 or +1, and the flips through 0 are where false signals cluster. Going all-in on a fresh flip buys every false start at full size; the ramp buys it at a fraction.
  • Among scaled rules, the shape barely matters. Every ramp starting between 0 and 0.3 and reaching full size between 0.75 and 1.0, linear or curved, scored Sharpe 2.19–2.22. That is a flat plateau, and the differences are noise. Fast-start curves (concave, or a ramp starting below 0) were worse, and step ladders were slightly worse than a smooth ramp. Balanced's 0.10 → 1.00 linear ramp sits in the middle of the plateau, so it stays.
  • The real lever is maximum exposure. Ramps that end above 1.0 (e.g. 0.2 → 1.5) never reach full size, because the score tops out at 1. They show higher Sharpe (≈2.30) and smaller drawdowns (−17%) but much lower CAGR (≈95%). This works like holding cash permanently, not like a better signal. "Lowest Drawdown" already uses it (0.10 → 1.25).
  • The risk-off residual added about 0.3 Sharpe under every exposure rule. Re-test on live data with "MTPI exposure study" in the Backtest Lab.

Rebalancing rule (Oct-2026 study)

  • Rule: every 5 days, bring every holding back to its RSPS target weight, even if nothing in the ranking changed. Between those dates, do nothing and let positions drift. MTPI state changes, and the risk-off trend residual, still trade immediately.
  • Why not "only trade when the RSPS changes": on real data that rule scored a lower Sharpe than a fixed 5-day cycle (Institutional 1.44 vs 1.68; Original 1.10 vs 1.29). The RSPS holdings change every 4–5 days on average, so the rule still trades almost as often, but it trades on the day of each flip, and daily flips in crypto tend to partly reverse. Letting winners drift without trimming also scored lower at every cadence tested (3, 5 and 7 days). Bringing a winner back to its volatility-adjusted cap is what keeps the risk budget intact.
  • Why 5 days and not 7, 10 or 14: longer cycles had similar or slightly higher average Sharpe, but the result depended heavily on which weekday the cycle started (Sharpe 1.24 to 2.12 for a weekly rule). The 5-day rule is the most consistent: Sharpe 1.50–1.85 across start days for Institutional, 1.21–1.35 for Original. It beats 3 days in every robustness test except the second half, where they tie.
  • Re-run the "Rebalancing rule study" in the Backtest Lab after big changes to the system; it tests every rule on your live data.

Trend tab & Current Model Portfolio

  • Trend tab: for every asset, the average of your three RSI models (RSI 14, RSI Standard Deviation 21/35, Momentum RSI 12 with 9/21 EMAs), each voting +1 above 50 and −1 below. The background is green when the average is above 0 and red when below; the darker shade means 3/3 agree. The lower panel shows a volatility-based "probable range" that approximates 42 Macro's proprietary one.
  • Current Model Portfolio (top of the RSPS page): a KISS-style positioning table, with each holding's percent of maximum exposure (its dynamic cap), its trend state, the change since the prior close, and 6-month betas to BTC and the S&P 500. The trend model is shown for information only: it does not change the RSPS weights.
  • Crypto trend readings update live with the RSPS feed. ETFs, the dollar index and yields come from a snapshot, so ask Claude to refresh it.

Portfolio page (multi-asset backtest)

  • What it is: a strategic-allocation backtester for BTC + VT + TLT + GLDM + REET/VNQ + cash, built the way an Australian investor would hold them: ETFs through IBKR in USD, BTC on an Australian exchange in AUD. It includes real IBKR commissions, spreads, FX conversion, 15% US withholding and, optionally, Australian CGT.
  • Bitcoin's early years dominate long backtests. From 2010, even a 5% BTC weight contributes close to half the total return; check the attribution table. Use the "Liquid BTC (2014)" and "All ETFs live (2018)" start buttons before sizing BTC.
  • Crash table: the GFC row uses the pre-BTC extended history (2004–2010), with the BTC weight held in cash by default. Pick "Spread its weight over the other assets" in the assumptions to redistribute it instead.
  • Weight explorer: the "best" mixes are in-sample. Prefer broad plateaus and check them across start dates.
  • Domicile: US-listed ETFs can expose a non-US person to US estate tax above US$60k. Consider Irish-domiciled or ASX-listed equivalents (general information, not advice).

Operational checklist

  1. Trade after the 00:00 UTC daily close (10–11am Sydney, depending on daylight saving). Open the dashboard, check the data date on the trade plan matches yesterday, and check the status shows no stale data.
  2. Rebalance on the scheduled days shown in the trade plan, or immediately when the MTPI state changes.
  3. Skip trades smaller than about 0.5 percentage points; they cost more than they're worth.
  4. Execute small caps (HB slots, ZEC, etc.) with limit orders or TWAP. On thin books, a market order can cost far more than the 10 bp assumed.
  5. Keep the MTPI TradingView log current, and save your settings (they are stored in this browser only, so clearing site data resets them).
  6. Review the Base Caps and preset quarterly at most, not after every bad week. Changing settings after drawdowns is the most common way systematic strategies are ruined.

Other risks to keep in mind

  • Counterparty / custody. Exchange insolvency or withdrawal freezes are the largest non-market risk. Consider splitting across venues and keeping long-term holdings in self-custody.
  • Tax (Australia). Every rebalance is generally a CGT event, and holdings under 12 months don't get the 50% discount. A 3-day rebalance creates many short-term disposals. Keep records and speak to a tax adviser. This is general information, not advice.
  • Correlation in crashes. Diversification across 4 crypto assets largely disappears in a market-wide crash; estimated portfolio vol is a calm-market number.
  • Listing / delisting. An asset that is delisted or changes ticker (as ZRO → ZROL) can break its price feed. If an asset shows no data, it is excluded automatically, so check the rank table.
  • Browser dependence. Prices come straight from the exchange APIs into your browser. A VPN or regional block (Binance is restricted in some places) can stop updates. The status bar will say so.
